claim: The developmental form of Trypanosoma brucei that infects mammals has a quorum sensing pathway that senses cell density and results in a G1/G0 arrest.
source: The developmental form of Trypanosoma brucei that infects mammals has a quorum sensing pathway that senses cell density and results in a G1/G0 arrest.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T. brucei biology presented as background information.

claim: The G1/G0 arrest in T. brucei is associated with both metabolic and morphological changes that cause proliferating 'slender' forms to differentiate into cell cycle-arrested 'stumpy' cells.
source: This arrest is associated with both metabolic and morphological changes that cause proliferating 'slender' forms to differentiate into cell cycle-arrested 'stumpy' cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about T. brucei differentiation presented as background.

claim: After passage through the tsetse fly and transition through various developmental forms, trypanosomes reach the salivary glands where the form able to infect mammals (metacyclic trypomastigotes) arises.
source: After passage through the tsetse fly and transition through various developmental forms, the trypanosomes reach the salivary glands. Here, the form able to infect mammals (metacyclic trypomastigotes) arises.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the T. brucei life cycle in the tsetse fly vector.

claim: Stumpy cells are able to initiate and complete the life cycle in the tsetse fly.
source: It is clear that stumpy cells are able to initiate and complete this cycle in the fly.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Slender forms can infect and complete the life cycle in tsetse flies with a comparable efficiency to stumpy forms under laboratory conditions.
source: Our observations and measurements show that slender forms can infect and complete the life cycle in tsetse flies with a comparable efficiency to stumpy forms under laboratory conditions.
evidence: This is the main finding of the authors' original paper, supported by their experimental data.

claim: When infected with only two trypanosomes per bloodmeal (~100 trypanosomes/ml blood), the stumpy stage is four times more effective in colonising the midgut.
source: When infected with only two trypanosomes per bloodmeal (~100 trypanosomes/ml blood), the stumpy stage is actually four times more effective in colonising the midgut, but only two times more effective in colonising the salivary glands.
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' experiments.

claim: When infected with only two trypanosomes per bloodmeal (~100 trypanosomes/ml blood), the stumpy stage is two times more effective in colonising the salivary glands.
source: When infected with only two trypanosomes per bloodmeal (~100 trypanosomes/ml blood), the stumpy stage is actually four times more effective in colonising the midgut, but only two times more effective in colonising the salivary glands.
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' experiments.

claim: When twenty trypanosomes were in the bloodmeal (~1000 trypanosomes/ml blood), the midguts were infected with virtually the same efficiency by slender and stumpy forms.
source: However, when twenty trypanosomes were in the bloodmeal (~1000 trypanosomes/ml blood), the midguts were infected with virtually the same efficiency, while the twofold difference in salivary gland infections remained.
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' experiments.

claim: When twenty trypanosomes were in the bloodmeal (~1000 trypanosomes/ml blood), the twofold difference in salivary gland infections between stumpy and slender forms remained.
source: However, when twenty trypanosomes were in the bloodmeal (~1000 trypanosomes/ml blood), the midguts were infected with virtually the same efficiency, while the twofold difference in salivary gland infections remained.
evidence: This is based on data from the authors' experiments.

claim: At a blood parasitaemia as low as 10³ cells/ml, there is no 'survivorship bias' in the midgut.
source: Thus, there is no 'survivorship bias' in the midgut at a blood parasitaemia as low as 103 cells/ml.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar midgut infection rates at this parasitemia level.

claim: At a parasitemia of 10³ cells/ml, stumpy forms would not be predominant in the trypanosome population.
source: At a parasitemia of 103 cells/ml, as simulated in our experiment, the stumpy forms would certainly not be predominant in the trypanosome population.
evidence: This is inferred from knowledge of trypanosome population dynamics at low parasitemia levels.

claim: The conditions used for transmission (infecting flies with their first bloodmeal and the inclusion of N-acetylglucosamine in the feed) are standard for lab infection of tsetse flies with trypanosomes.
source: The conditions used for transmission (infecting flies with their first bloodmeal and the inclusion of N-acetylglucosamine in the feed) are standard for lab infection of tsetse flies with trypanosomes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about standard laboratory protocols.

claim: The dependency of tsetse fly age/feeding history on infection rate is known, but not fully understood.
source: The dependency of tsetse fly age/feeding history on infection rate is known, but not fully understood (Haines, 2013; Leak, 1998), and it is likely that flies are more easily infected when they take their first bloodmeal (Leak, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Flies are likely more easily infected when they take their first bloodmeal.
source: The dependency of tsetse fly age/feeding history on infection rate is known, but not fully understood (Haines, 2013; Leak, 1998), and it is likely that flies are more easily infected when they take their first bloodmeal (Leak, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Leak, 1998.

claim: For the tsetse experiments, the authors used freshly hatched (teneral) flies, as is routinely done by other tsetse laboratories.
source: For the tsetse experiments, we used freshly hatched (teneral) flies, as is routinely done by other tsetse laboratories (Haines, 2013; Leak, 1998).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used and is supported by citations showing this is standard practice.

claim: N-acetylglucosamine is generally used for tsetse infection experiments, but is not required for infection.
source: Likewise, N-acetylglucosamine is generally used, but is not required for infection (Imhof et al., 2014; Peacock et al., 2012; Shaw et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Currently, nobody knows the exact transmission dynamics in regions where trypanosomes are endemic, and what additional environmental parameters take effect there.
source: Currently, nobody knows the exact transmission dynamics in regions where trypanosomes are endemic, and what additional environmental parameters take effect there.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: No cell cycle arrest at all is required for the direct differentiation from the slender form to the procyclic insect stage, neither in vivo nor in vitro.
source: This seems odd, as we have shown that no cell cycle arrest at all is required for the direct differentiation from the slender form to the procyclic insect stage, neither in vivo nor in vitro.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: In vitro, the transition from dividing slender parasites to the procyclic insect stage occurs in the absence of quorum sensing, and is solely triggered by cold-shock and cis-aconitate addition.
source: Note that, in vitro, the transition from dividing slender parasites to the procyclic insect stage occurs in the absence of quorum sensing, and is solely triggered by cold-shock and cis-aconitate addition (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Slender trypanosomes in a continuously dividing population activate the PAD1 pathway in vivo upon uptake by the tsetse fly.
source: Slender trypanosomes in a continuously dividing population activate the PAD1 pathway in vivo upon uptake by the tsetse fly.
evidence: This is the title of Figure 1 and is supported by the data shown in that figure.

claim: Slender cell populations continuously divide while turning on the PAD1 pathway, seamlessly transitioning into the first fly form.
source: Slender cell populations continuously divide while turning on the PAD1 pathway, seamlessly transitioning into the first fly form.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in the figure data.

claim: Stumpy cell populations do not start to divide until 48 hours after uptake, after they have started to become the first fly form.
source: Stumpy cell populations do not start to divide until 48 after uptake, after they have started to become the first fly form.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 legend and shown in the figure data.

claim: In the in vivo experiment, 1845 slender cells were analyzed.
source: Slender cells (n = 1845) are shown in dark grey bars, and stumpy cells (n = 1237) are shown in light grey bars.
evidence: This is the sample size reported in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: In the in vivo experiment, 1237 stumpy cells were analyzed.
source: Slender cells (n = 1845) are shown in dark grey bars, and stumpy cells (n = 1237) are shown in light grey bars.
evidence: This is the sample size reported in the Figure 1 legend.

claim: Slender trypanosomes activate the PAD1 pathway in vitro in a continuously dividing population.
source: Slender trypanosomes activate the PAD1 pathway in vitro in a continuously dividing population.
evidence: This is the title of Figure 2 and is supported by the data shown in that figure.

claim: Slender cell populations continuously divided while transiently turning on the PAD1 pathway, showing no cell cycle arrest.
source: Slender cell populations continuously divided while transiently turning on the PAD1 pathway, showing no cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend and shown in the figure data.

claim: Stumpy cell populations did not start to divide as procyclic forms until 48 hours after cis-aconitate addition.
source: Stumpy cell populations did not start to divide as procyclic forms until 48 after cis-aconitate addition.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 2 legend and shown in the figure data.

claim: In the in vitro experiment, 1653 slender cells were analyzed.
source: Slender cells (n = 1653) are shown in dark grey and stumpy cells (n = 1798) in light gray.
evidence: This is the sample size reported in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: In the in vitro experiment, 1798 stumpy cells were analyzed.
source: Slender cells (n = 1653) are shown in dark grey and stumpy cells (n = 1798) in light gray.
evidence: This is the sample size reported in the Figure 2 legend.

claim: T. congolense is a sympatric trypanosome species which does not develop a morphologically distinct stumpy form but does contain a complete set of quorum sensing pathway genes.
source: T. congolense is a sympatric trypanosome species which does not develop a morphologically distinct stumpy form but does contain a complete set of quorum sensing pathway genes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about T. congolense biology.

claim: Infections of flies with low numbers of T. congolense are possible.
source: Matthews and Larcombe take this as further evidence that no morphological transition is necessary to infect the tsetse fly (Silvester et al., 2017), and note that infections of flies with low numbers of T. congolense are possible.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Silvester et al., 2017.

claim: The stumpy stage can predominate in chronic mouse infections, with trypanosomes reaching population densities exceeding 1 × 10⁷ cells/ml as differentiation occurs.
source: The standard laboratory model of infection is the mouse and there is no doubt that the stumpy stage can predominate in chronic mouse infections, with trypanosomes reaching population densities exceeding 1 × 107 cells/ml as differentiation occurs (MacGregor et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacGregor et al., 2011.

claim: In endemic areas, large mammals are the main host and all evidence indicates that trypanosome numbers remain well below 1 × 10⁷ cells/ml density.
source: In endemic areas, large mammals are the main host and all evidence indicates that trypanosome numbers remain well below this density (Frezil, 1971; Koch, 1909; Mbaya et al., 2009; Mbaya et al., 2008; Mehlitz and Molyneux, 2019; Wombou Toukam et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to field studies.

claim: Robert Koch quantified trypanosomes in 1906/7 during an epidemic of the human disease, with trypanosome numbers between 20 and 100 parasites/ml of human blood.
source: Robert Koch quantified trypanosomes in 1906/7 during an epidemic of the human disease, with trypanosome numbers between 20 and 100 parasites/ml of human blood (Koch, 1909; Schuster et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koch, 1909 and Schuster et al., 2021.

claim: The trypanosome population density in the blood simply does not reach numbers that make a quorum sensing-driven differentiation likely.
source: The trypanosome population density in the blood simply does not reach numbers that make a quorum sensing-driven differentiation likely (Schuster et al., 2021, Appendix 1).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Schuster et al., 2021, Appendix 1.

claim: In wild animals, parasite numbers in the blood are often so low that transmission dependent solely on the stumpy stage seems extremely unlikely.
source: Furthermore, in wild animals, parasite numbers in the blood are often so low that transmission dependent solely on the stumpy stage seems extremely unlikely (Mbaya et al., 2009; Mbaya et al., 2008; Mehlitz and Molyneux, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to field studies and represents an inference from the data.

claim: In the mammalian host, slender and stumpy trypanosomes have clearly separate roles.
source: In the mammalian host, slender and stumpy trypanosomes have clearly separate roles; in the tsetse fly, these functions converge to the single goal of ensuring passage through the definitive host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about trypanosome biology.

claim: In the tsetse fly, the functions of slender and stumpy trypanosomes converge to the single goal of ensuring passage through the definitive host.
source: In the mammalian host, slender and stumpy trypanosomes have clearly separate roles; in the tsetse fly, these functions converge to the single goal of ensuring passage through the definitive host.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the authors' data and reasoning.

claim: The cell cycle-arrested stumpy life cycle stage is evolutionarily conserved in T. brucei to regulate the parasite load in the host and to allow persistent and disseminating infections with proliferating slender forms.
source: The cell cycle-arrested stumpy life cycle stage is evolutionarily conserved in T. brucei to regulate the parasite load in the host and to allow persistent and disseminating infections with proliferating slender forms.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge and evolutionary reasoning.

claim: The PAD1-pathway is already triggered in stumpy cells while in the mammalian host.
source: The first one, the PAD1-pathway, is already triggered in stumpy cells while in the mammalian host.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the PAD1 pathway.

claim: The PAD1 pathway being triggered in stumpy cells while in the mammalian host is potentially to initiate the preparation of the short-lived stumpy cell for transmission to the fly.
source: This is potentially to initiate the preparation of the short-lived stumpy cell for transmission to the fly (Quintana et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Quintana et al., 2021.

claim: The differentiation in the tsetse fly is not restricted to stumpy trypanosomes and the pathway can be launched in slender trypanosomes in the fly.
source: We have shown that the differentiation in the tsetse fly is not restricted to stumpy trypanosomes and that the pathway can be launched in slender trypanosomes in the fly.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' experimental data.

claim: The PAD1 pathway activation in slender trypanosomes occurs immediately after uptake by the tsetse fly.
source: This occurs immediately after uptake, and the slender cells which have activated the PAD1 pathway then differentiate directly to the procyclic insect stage.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental data.

claim: Slender cells which have activated the PAD1 pathway differentiate directly to the procyclic insect stage.
source: This occurs immediately after uptake, and the slender cells which have activated the PAD1 pathway then differentiate directly to the procyclic insect stage.
evidence: This is based on the authors' experimental data.

claim: Phenotypic plasticity in parasitic lifestyles, as seen with trypanosome adipose tissue forms and skin tissue forms, is an understudied but fundamental aspect of parasitism.
source: We are convinced that phenotypic plasticity in parasitic lifestyles, as seen with trypanosome adipose tissue forms and skin tissue forms, is an understudied but fundamental aspect of parasitism (Capewell et al., 2016; Reuter et al., 2021; Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to recent research on tissue forms.

claim: The authors used the transmission index introduced by Peacock and colleagues to quantify the success of transmission.
source: Therefore, the completion of the journey through the fly seems the logical way of quantifying the success of transmission and was the reason we used the transmission index introduced by Peacock and colleagues (Peacock et al., 2012).
evidence: This describes the methodology used and is supported by citation.

claim: Even monomorphic parasites readily infect the midgut, but never reach the salivary glands.
source: Even monomorphic parasites readily infect the midgut, after all, but never reach the salivary glands.
evidence: This is established knowledge about monomorphic trypanosome strains.

claim: Transmission mainly by teneral flies might be an evolutionary advantage for the parasite, as this reduces the burden on the vector and avoids competition between trypanosome strains and species.
source: Biologically, it would even make sense that transmission mainly by teneral flies might be an evolutionary advantage for the parasite, as this reduces the burden on the vector and avoids competition between trypanosome strains and species.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning about evolutionary advantages.

claim: If both slender and stumpy trypanosomes can infect the fly, this provides another potential solution to the transmission paradox, along with trypanosomes in the skin.
source: However, if we assume that both slender and stumpy trypanosomes can infect the fly, for which we present evidence, then another potential solution to the paradox, along with trypanosomes in the skin, is possible (Capewell et al., 2016; Trindade et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' data and supported by citations about skin forms.

claim: Matthews and Larcombe argue that stumpy cells are no longer defined by either morphology or cell cycle arrest.
source: They argue instead that the observations are consistent with their alternative model in which stumpy cells are no longer defined by either morphology or cell cycle arrest.
evidence: This describes the position taken by Matthews and Larcombe in their comment.

claim: Matthews and Larcombe suggest that only the molecular pathway which triggers stumpy formation on the way to becoming a procyclic is required to define a stumpy cell.
source: In the most intriguing part of their comment, Matthews and Larcombe argue that the stumpy stage should no longer be defined by morphology or cell cycle arrest. Instead, they suggest that only the molecular pathway which triggers stumpy formation on the way to becoming a procyclic is required.
evidence: This describes the position taken by Matthews and Larcombe in their comment.

claim: By Matthews and Larcombe's definition, a morphologically slender cell which has activated expression of PAD1 or other components of this pathway should be recognised as a stumpy cell.
source: By this definition, a morphologically slender cell, which has activated expression of PAD1 or other components of this pathway, should be recognised as a stumpy cell – regardless of its appearance, cell cycle status, or the transient nature of PAD1 expression.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of Matthews and Larcombe's proposed definition.

claim: The authors favour a model with an unexpected phenotypic plasticity for the slender stage and a certain degree of stochasticity in the trypanosome life cycle.
source: Hence, we favour a model with an unexpected phenotypic plasticity for the slender stage and a certain degree of stochasticity in the trypanosome life cycle.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation of their data.

claim: The first interpretation (phenotypic plasticity for the slender stage) would not falsify any published work.
source: While the first interpretation – which we favour – would not falsify any published work, the second one – which Matthews and Larcombe are proposing – would contradict the literature.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of different interpretations.

claim: The second interpretation (radical redefinition of stumpy stage) would contradict the literature.
source: While the first interpretation – which we favour – would not falsify any published work, the second one – which Matthews and Larcombe are proposing – would contradict the literature.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of different interpretations.
